stops.name: Medellín, the house by the castle of the Counts
stops.campa: In the walled town of Medellín on the Guadiana, in the house of the hidalgo Martín Cortés de Monroy and Catalina Pizarro Altamirano, a sickly boy is born and put out to nurse with María de Esteban, whose milk the old chroniclers credit for the strength that saves him. He is baptized in the font of San Martín, under the castle of the Counts of Medellín. His mother's kin, the Pizarro Altamiranos of nearby Trujillo, share blood with a cousin still a child there, Francisco Pizarro: two boys of this same hard Extremadura who will one day divide an ocean of empire between them.

stops.name: Salamanca, the law studies abandoned
stops.campa: At fourteen his father sends him to the schools of Salamanca to study Latin and law, lodging with kin near the university where the doctors of Roman and canon law hold their chairs. He reads two years of the Institutes and the Decretals, gaining a notary's Latin and an advocate's argument that will serve him better than any sword: the legal mind that drafts a city's charter out of a beachhead, that answers Rome and the Crown in their own tongue. But the schools cannot hold him. Restless and short of patience, he abandons the degree and goes home to Medellín, itching for the Indies.

stops.name: Santo Domingo, the notary lands
stops.campa: At nineteen he takes ship for Hispaniola, first island of the Ocean Sea, arriving at Santo Domingo under the governor Nicolás de Ovando, a kinsman of his mother's house. He had meant to sail earlier with Ovando's own fleet but broke an arm falling from a wall he climbed to see a married woman, and missed the ships. Registered a citizen of the new city, he is given a building lot and a repartimiento of Indians, learns the notary's trade and the sword together, and serves in the campaigns that finish subduing the island's remaining caciques.

stops.name: Azua, encomienda and the notary's table
stops.campa: Ovando plants him at Azua, a raw town on the island's dry south coast, as notary and encomendero, keeping the royal fifth's accounts and the register of branded Indian slaves. Six years he farms, mines a little gold, and quarrels with his neighbors as a man of spirit does in a small place: a fight over a debt nearly ends him at the point of a sword. He is a substantial nobody: alcalde's clerk, cattle-man, gambler, litigant. Diego Velázquez, governor of the province, marks him for his quick pen and his temper, and will not let him go idle for long.

stops.name: Maisí, Cuba: the conquest with Velázquez
stops.campa: Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, sent to complete the conquest of Cuba, takes Cortés as his secretary and accountant, and the small fleet lands near Maisí at the island's eastern point. The cacique Hatuey, fled from Hispaniola with tales of Spanish greed, resists to the death and is burned; the island's chiefdoms fall one by one behind him. Cortés serves close to the governor's person, drafting his letters, keeping his gold, learning at close range how a conquest is financed, provisioned, and written home about: an apprenticeship in command he will not forget when his own turn comes.

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba: alcalde, and Catalina Suárez
stops.campa: At Santiago, Velázquez's capital, Cortés rises to alcalde and man of substance, with cattle, a gold claim, an encomienda, but his tongue outruns his prudence: he conspires with malcontents against the governor's harsh dealing, is twice arrested, once escapes his own gaol by night and takes sanctuary in a church, and is reconciled to Velázquez only by marrying Catalina Suárez, sister-in-law of the governor's household, whom he had compromised and long refused. The marriage mends the quarrel outwardly; the wariness between the two men, the elder distrustful of the younger's ambition, never fully closes.

stops.name: Cozumel, the idols cast down
stops.campa: Named captain-general at last of an armada Velázquez already regrets giving him, Cortés sails from Cuba with eleven ships, five hundred men, and sixteen horses under a black banner sewn with a cross, bearing the device that this is the sign to follow with faith and victory will come. At Cozumel he finds a Maya shrine of the goddess Ixchel, has the idols thrown down and an altar of Our Lady raised in their place, and hears from island traders of bearded, tattered men held on the mainland: Christians, shipwrecked, kept as slaves for eight years among the lords of Yucatán.

stops.name: Cozumel, Jerónimo de Aguilar restored
stops.campa: Ransom and letters go by canoe to the mainland, and delay nearly costs the fleet its chance: a leaking ship forces Cortés back to Cozumel just as a canoe lands a bearded man in Maya dress, sunburned unrecognizable, carrying a breviary wrapped in a rag: Jerónimo de Aguilar, castaway of a wrecked caravel, eight years a slave to a Yucatec lord and keeper of his Christian prayers by memory alone. His companion Gonzalo Guerrero, tattooed and married among the Maya, sends word he will not come: he has a wife and children now. Aguilar's Maya tongue becomes the fleet's first ear into this country.

stops.name: Centla, Tabasco: the battle, Doña Marina given
stops.campa: At the mouth of the river of Tabasco the Chontal Maya of Potonchán attack in thousands and break against horses and cannon they have never seen. Survivors say afterward that centaurs fought among the strangers. The caciques sue for peace, and among gifts of gold and cloth give twenty young women. One, a Nahuatl noblewoman of Coatzacoalco sold into slavery as a child, is named Malinalli; baptized she becomes Doña Marina. Paired with Aguilar's Maya, her Nahuatl makes the fleet's true voice, and within months the Nahuas call Cortés himself Malinche, for the woman never absent from his side: La Malinche, the tongue of the whole conquest.
stops.quote: He querido declarar esto porque sin ir doña Marina no podíamos entender la lengua de la Nueva España y México.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 37

stops.name: San Juan de Ulúa: the landing, the Totonac embassies
stops.campa: On Holy Thursday the fleet anchors under the sand-island of San Juan de Ulúa, and the next day, Good Friday, the Spaniards step onto the mainland of what will be called New Spain for the first time. Governors of Moctezuma's empire come down from Cuetlaxtlan with food, cloth, and gold disks, and painters set to copying the strangers, their ships, their horses, in picture-writing to carry to Tenochtitlan. Cortés receives the embassy seated in state, has Mass said, and answers through Aguilar and Marina's double relay that he comes from a great king beyond the sea and must speak with their lord in person.

stops.name: Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, the town founded
stops.campa: Cortés sets aside Velázquez's commission on his own authority: has his soldiers 'elect' him captain-general and chief justice in the king's name directly, over the governor's head, and founds the Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz: the True Cross, first Spanish town on the mainland, with its alcaldes, its regidores, its royal fifth set aside before any gold is even won. It is a legal fiction built on a beach, but it is enough: from this hour Cortés answers to Charles V alone, and Velázquez's claim over him is, on paper, already dead.

stops.name: Cempoala, the fat cacique and the Totonac alliance
stops.campa: Inland at Cempoala, a garden city of white-plastered temples the soldiers first mistake for silver, the vastly stout cacique the men call 'the fat chief' receives them and unburdens himself: his Totonac people, like a score of subject nations, groan under Moctezuma's tribute-collectors and the yearly draft of youths for sacrifice. Cortés promises deliverance from the Aztec yoke in exchange for alliance and men, has the Totonac idols toppled from the great temple over the priests' horrified protest, and gains his first native army: seed of the coalition of the empire's enemies that will actually take Tenochtitlan.
